title: Turkish Drone Strike in Somali Border Town Detonates a Federal Crisis; Ankara Probes Ex-PM Davutoglu as Aegean Friction Mounts
subhead: A reported Turkish strike on a former Somali general's home in Doolow has pitted Mogadishu against Jubaland and drawn calls for an independent probe, while Ankara opens an insult probe into former PM Davutoglu and keeps pressure on Greece over the Aegean and Evros.

sections.heading: Somalia: Doolow Drone Strike Turns a Patron Relationship Into a Political Liability
sections.body: A reported Turkish drone strike on the residence of a former Somali general in Doolow, in the Gedo region near the Ethiopian border, has triggered the sharpest test yet of Ankara's deepening footprint in Somalia. Multiple Somali outlets, including Garowe Online, Hiiraan Online and Horn Observer, report that the strike targeted the home of a former corrections commander (variously identified as Gen. Mahad and linked to Gen. Shub) and set off a direct clash of accounts between Jubaland and the federal government in Mogadishu. Jubaland condemned the strike, while Mogadishu denied involvement, according to FTL Somalia and Horn Observer. The Somali opposition coalition and several former presidents have called for an independent investigation, and protests have erupted in the Gedo region, per Horn Observer. The political fallout escalated further when former NISA chief Fahad Yasin publicly linked the strike to Somalia's new parliamentary speaker, an allegation reported by Sunatimes and somaliguardian.com. The Times of Israel and Horseed Media frame the episode as Ankara sliding from 'Somali patron' to 'Villa Somalia's hired gun.'
sections.whyItMatters: Turkey's signature Somali assets — a large military base in Mogadishu, the Doolow-area presence and a Bayraktar drone fleet operating alongside Somali forces — are now entangled in Somalia's internal federal-vs-state struggle. If Ankara is seen as doing Mogadishu's dirty work against Jubaland, it risks alienating the regional states and Ethiopian-facing constituencies that its Africa strategy depends on.

sections.heading: Domestic Politics: Insult Probe Opened Against Former PM Davutoglu
sections.body: Turkish prosecutors have opened an investigation into Ahmet Davutoglu, the former prime minister and one-time close ally of President Erdogan who later became an opposition leader, over alleged 'insult to the president' in 2021 remarks, according to Bloombberg, Turkish Minute, Hürriyet Daily News and Middle East Monitor. Asharq Al-Awsat notes the probe targets remarks made years earlier, signaling a long memory on the insult statute (Article 299 of the penal code). The development comes weeks after Davutoglu announced he was stepping back from active politics, a departure timeline documented by Al Jazeera and Middle East Eye.
sections.whyItMatters: Reopening a years-old insult case against a now-retreating former premier reads less as a personal vendetta than a signal to the broader opposition and ex-AKP figures that leaving politics does not immunize them from prosecution. It also reinforces the legal pressure toolkit Ankara has used against critics.

sections.heading: Aegean: 'Blue Homeland' Rhetoric, UAV Overflights and the Evros Fence
sections.body: Greece-Turkey friction has sharpened on multiple fronts. eKathimerini reports Turkish UAV overflights are now being recorded daily, and that Ankara has formally protested Athens' extension of the border fence along the Evros river — with AzerNews reporting Turkey sent a diplomatic note over the Evros fence. The two sides also remain at odds over Turkish marine parks in disputed waters, which Greece rejected, and Greek PM Mitsotakis warned Ankara it will 'take no instructions on sovereignty or defense' (GreekReporter). The row follows an escalation in Turkish media and presidential rhetoric invoking the 'Blue Homeland' doctrine and threats toward Greek islands, covered by Greek City Times and Ynet. Israel Hayom frames the episode partly as a byproduct of Greece's Israeli-built air-defense infrastructure shifting the regional balance.
sections.whyItMatters: These are mostly coercive-diplomatic moves — drones, notes, marine-park claims — rather than kinetic escalation, but they keep Aegean sovereignty disputes live at a time when Athens has deepened its defense ties with Israel and Turkey is juggling crises in Somalia and with Washington.

sections.heading: US-Iran Bank Sanctions: Ankara Absorbs the Blow and Pivots to Mediation
sections.body: The US Treasury sanctions on a Turkish bank over alleged Iran-linked oil-revenue transfers — the story that dominated Friday's brief — continued to reverberate over the weekend. Fortune detailed the US accusation that the bank helped Iran move oil revenue from China to Turkey, while i24NEWS reported a US envoy moved to reassure Ankara after the measure. Ankara's public posture remains de-escalatory: TRT World and Hürriyet Daily News both quote President Erdogan saying Türkiye is working to end US-Iran tensions, including in a call with the UAE leadership. This diplomatic framing follows Turkey's reported role as a go-between in Washington-Tehran channels.
sections.whyItMatters: Turkey is trying to contain the financial damage of the sanctions by casting itself as a mediator rather than a target, but the Treasury action still puts a real cost on Ankara's trade ties to Iran just as Washington dangles F-35 sales and sanctions relief in the background.

sections.heading: Mecca Pact: A 'Muslim NATO' Narrative Gains Traction in Western Media
sections.body: The Turkey-Saudi Arabia-Pakistan defense arrangement continued to draw attention, with The Washington Times framing it as a 'Muslim NATO' born of concerns over US reliability and Israel's rise, following the pact's first meeting in Istanbul late last month. Euractiv reported Brussels is warming to the so-called 'Mecca' defense pact despite Chinese espionage concerns, while SCMP noted Bangladesh's flirtation with the grouping is raising red flags in India. The Times of India reported Pakistan is set to lead the grouping for an initial three-year term.
sections.whyItMatters: The grouping is a hedge against perceived US unreliability in the Gulf and wider region, but its practical substance — joint exercises, procurement, command — remains thin. For Ankara it reinforces the image of an independent, multi-aligned security pole without committing to formal obligations that could complicate NATO membership.

sections.heading: Energy & Infrastructure: Turkey and AIIB Sign Cooperation Deal on Marine Cleanup
sections.body: Turkey and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) signed a cooperation deal, with the first focus on marine cleaning, finance minister Simsek said, according to Reuters and TRT World, which described it as a multi-million-dollar environment agreement. The move deepens Turkey's engagement with the Beijing-led development bank as part of its broader pivot toward Asian financing channels.
sections.whyItMatters: Modest in size, the AIIB deal is strategically notable for the signal it sends: Turkey is actively diversifying its external financing away from Western-dominated institutions at a moment when US Treasury sanctions complicate Western capital access.

bottomLine: The dominant new development is in Somalia, where a reported Turkish drone strike in Doolow has embroiled Ankara in a federal-vs-regional political crisis with protest and probe calls — a real cost attached to Turkey's most visible African military footprint. At home, the insult investigation into former PM Davutoglu signals the legal pressure on critics is intact, while Aegean friction with Greece continues to simmer through drones, diplomatic notes and marine-park claims. The US-Iran bank sanctions and the Mecca Pact remain live but incremental. Together the day's threads show a Turkey managing multiple simultaneous pressures — Horn of Africa entanglement, domestic legal pressure, Aegean coercion and financial exposure to Washington — without any single one yet escalating into a decisive break.
